content: 1. Hahmanesh M et al. conducted a study on the use of valacyclovir for suppressing recurrent genital herpes in individuals infected with the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). The findings were published in the Journal of Infectious Diseases in 2003, volume 188, issue 7, pages 1009–1016. 2. Dunne EF and colleagues investigated the effects of suppressive acyclovir therapy on reducing HIV shedding in the cervicovaginal region of women co-infected with HIV and herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2) in Chiang Rai, Thailand. The results were published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2008, volume 49, issue 1, pages 77–83. 3. Mayaud P et al. examined the impact of acyclovir on genital and plasma HIV-1 RNA levels, HSV-2 DNA, and ulcer healing in African women with HIV-1 and herpes ulcers. This randomized placebo-controlled trial was published in the Journal of Infectious Diseases in 2009, volume 200, issue 2, pages 216–226. 4. The Partners in Prevention HSV/HIV Transmission Study Team conducted a randomized controlled trial to assess the efficacy of daily acyclovir in reducing HSV-2 transmission from individuals co-infected with HSV-2 and HIV-1. The findings were published in the Journal of Infectious Diseases in 2013, volume 208, issue 9, pages 1366–1374. 5. Nagot N et al. demonstrated that suppressive therapy targeting HSV can reduce HIV-1 RNA levels. Their study was published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2007, volume 356, issue 8, pages 790–799. 6. Nijhawan AE and colleagues conducted a pilot randomized controlled trial to evaluate the effect of HSV-2 suppressive therapy on genital tract HIV-1 RNA shedding in women receiving highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART). The results were published in Infectious Diseases in Obstetrics and Gynecology in 2012. 7. Ouedraogo A et al. assessed the impact of suppressive herpes therapy on genital HIV-1 RNA levels in women undergoing antiretroviral therapy. This randomized controlled trial was published in AIDS in 2006, volume 20, issue 18, pages 2305–2313. 8. Paz-Bailey G et al. investigated the improvement in ulcer healing and reduction in HIV shedding with episodic acyclovir therapy as part of syndromic management in men. The study was published in the Journal of Infectious Diseases in 2009, volume 200, issue 7, pages 1039–1049. 9. Phiri S et al. studied the effects of acyclovir on ulcer healing, lesion resolution, and genital and plasma HIV-1 RNA levels in patients with genital ulcer disease in Malawi. The findings were published in Sexually Transmitted Infections in 2010, volume 86, issue 5, pages 345–352. 10. Reynolds SJ et al. conducted a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial to evaluate the effect of daily acyclovir on HIV disease progression in individuals co-infected with HIV-1 and HSV-2 in Rakai, Uganda. The study was published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases in 2012, volume 12, issue 6, pages 441–448. 11. Romanowski B et al., as part of the Collaborative Famciclovir HIV Study Group, assessed the efficacy and safety of famciclovir for treating mucocutaneous herpes simplex infections in HIV-infected individuals. The results were published in AIDS in 2000, volume 14, issue 9, pages 1211–1217. 12. Schacker T et al. conducted a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial to evaluate famciclovir for suppressing symptomatic and asymptomatic herpes simplex virus reactivation in HIV-infected individuals. The findings were published in the Annals of Internal Medicine in 1998, volume 128, issue 1, pages 21–28. 13. Tanton C et al. investigated the long-term impact of acyclovir suppressive therapy on genital and plasma HIV RNA levels in Tanzanian women. This randomized controlled trial was published in the Journal of Infectious Diseases in 2010, volume 201, issue 9, pages 1285–1297.
